lugbara_dribidu.name: Receives fire and medicine-knowledge from the woman of the land
lugbara_dribidu.notes: On entering the present Lugbara land Dribidu, like his counterpart Jaki, received fire from a local woman whom he then married; he passed magical medicines (including rain-medicine) to his descendants.

sources.reference: John Middleton, Lugbara Religion (1960); Wikipedia, 'Lugbara mythology'

lugbara_dribidu.name: Devours his own children and is driven into exile
lugbara_dribidu.notes: In his hero-ancestor cycle Dribidu the hairy one ate his own children, earning the byname Banyale ('eater of men'); exiled for the cannibalism, he died on Mount Eti.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Lugbara mythology'; Middleton, Lugbara Religion (1960)

lugbara_jaki.name: Brings the first rain-medicine into Lugbara land
lugbara_jaki.notes: Jaki is one of the two original Lugbara rainmakers (paired with Dribidu), whose mastery of magical medicines for calling rain was inherited by the clans he founded.

sources.reference: John Middleton, Lugbara Religion (1960); Wikipedia, 'Lugbara mythology'

lugbara_jaki.name: Fathers the sons who found the major Lugbara clans
lugbara_jaki.notes: After receiving fire from and marrying a woman of the land, Jaki fathered many sons who became the eponymous founders of the principal Lugbara clans; he died on Mount Liru.

sources.reference: John Middleton, Lugbara Religion (1960)

luo_nyasaye.name: Grants prosperity, fertility and rain to those who sacrifice
luo_nyasaye.notes: As high-god the Luo invoke Nyasaye at sacred places (hembko) with spotless animal offerings to secure rain, fertility, health and continued prosperity, and to avert calamity (dera).

sources.reference: R. Oduor, 'Nyasaye — God for the Luo People' (2019); Exploring-Africa, 'Luo religious beliefs'

luo_juogi.name: Act as good or evil spirits, known or unknown
luo_juogi.notes: The juogi (from jok) divide into beneficent and malevolent classes, and into known (named ancestral) and unknown spirits; they mediate between the living and the divine, protect kin, and afflict the negligent.

sources.reference: Exploring-Africa, 'Luo religious beliefs'; IJRISS, 'Elements of Luo Traditional Sacrifice'

luo_ramogi.name: Leads the Luo from Pubungu and founds the first settlement at Got Ramogi
luo_ramogi.notes: Ramogi Ajwang' led the Nilotic Luo out of Pubungu/Pakwach and settled at the Ramogi Hills in Siaya, traditionally remembered as the dispersal-point and first home of the Kenyan Luo.

sources.reference: IJISRT, 'Luo Cultural Shrines: The Hembko of Got Ramogi, Kenya' (2024); Kenyans.co.ke, 'Why Got Ramogi Holds a Special Place in Luo Heritage'

luwian_kamrusepa.name: Acts as divine midwife and inventor of healing ritual
luwian_kamrusepa.notes: Beyond curing illness, Kamrusepa is credited in Luwian incantations from Kizzuwatna as the originator of ritual procedures later handed to humans, and could function as a divine midwife.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Kamrušepa'; Hutter, in Melchert (ed.), The Luwians (2003)

lydian_artimus.name: Brings destruction on whoever damages a protected grave
lydian_artimus.notes: In Lydian funerary curse formulae (e.g. the Sardis bilingual) Artimus of Sardis and of Koloe/Ephesos is invoked to bring ruin upon anyone who harms the tomb, its dromos or its belongings, extending the curse to the violator's house, court, land and water.

sources.reference: Sardis bilingual Lydian-Aramaic inscription (stele of Maneś son of Kumliś, 4th c. BC)
Wikipedia, 'Iyarri'; Hutter, in Melchert (ed.), The Luwians (2003)

lusitanian_endovelicus.name: Dream-incubation and votive cult at São Miguel da Mota
lusitanian_endovelicus.notes: At the sanctuary near Terena (Alandroal) supplicants sought healing and oracular answers through incubatio (sleeping in the precinct); about 92 Latin votive inscriptions survive, often with formulae ex responsu or ex imperato, alongside bronze and terracotta figurines, boar sculptures and even surgical instruments.

sources.reference: Votive inscriptions of the Endovellicus sanctuary, São Miguel da Mota (CIL II); excavation reports (Schattner et al., 2002)

lusitanian_ataecina.name: Curse-tablet and votive cult of Ataecina Turibrigensis
lusitanian_ataecina.notes: Worshippers dedicated goat-figurines welded to inscribed plaques (Santa Lucía del Trampal, Malpartida, Herguijuela) and deposited binding curse-tablets; the Mérida defixio invokes 'Dea Ataecina Turibrigensis Proserpina' to avenge stolen garments. Her cult centred on the lost town of Turobriga in Celtic Beturia.

sources.reference: Mérida defixio (CIL II 462); votive goat-plaques of Cáceres province

lusitanian_bormanicus.name: Thermal-spring healing dedications at Caldas de Vizela
lusitanian_bormanicus.notes: Votive altars dedicated to Bormanico (and to the syncretic Reo Bormanico) were set up at the hot springs of Caldas de Vizela in northern Portugal, the offerers seeking healing through the bubbling thermal water.

sources.reference: Votive inscriptions of Caldas de Vizela (CIL II)

lusitanian_reve.name: Bull-offering in the Cabeço das Fráguas sacrifice
lusitanian_reve.notes: In the Lusitanian suovetaurilia recorded on the Cabeço das Fráguas rock, Reve receives a breeding bull (the 'comaiam' / Reva), the climactic victim of the joint offering to the local gods.

sources.reference: Cabeço das Fráguas inscription (Lusitanian, Latin alphabet)

lusitanian_trebaruna.name: Yearling-sheep offering in the Cabeço das Fráguas sacrifice
lusitanian_trebaruna.notes: The Cabeço das Fráguas invocatio assigns Trebaruna a one-year-old sheep within the collective sacrifice; she is also widely attested on votive altars, sometimes paired with Reve.

sources.reference: Cabeço das Fráguas inscription; Lusitanian votive epigraphy

lusitanian_trebopala.name: Opening sheep of the Cabeço das Fráguas sacrifice
lusitanian_trebopala.notes: The invocatio opens 'one sheep to Trebopala', making her the first-named recipient of the joint Lusitanian offering ('Damos-te esta ovelha, ó Trebopala').

sources.reference: Cabeço das Fráguas inscription (invocatio)

lusitanian_laebo.name: Pig-offering in the Cabeço das Fráguas sacrifice
lusitanian_laebo.notes: In the same invocatio Laebo receives a pig ('a pig to Laebo'), the only defined cultic act for this otherwise obscure deity.

sources.reference: Cabeço das Fráguas inscription

lusitanian_iccona.name: Mare-offering at Cabeço das Fráguas
lusitanian_iccona.notes: Iccona Loiminna receives the offering of a mare in the Cabeço das Fráguas rite, consistent with her reconstruction as an Epona-like horse-goddess (*Ekwonā).

sources.reference: Cabeço das Fráguas inscription; Blázquez on Iccona Loiminna

lusitanian_nabia.name: Spring and river votive cult
lusitanian_nabia.notes: Nabia received numerous votive dedications across the Gallaecian-Lusitanian northwest, at springs and watercourses; at the Fonte do Ídolo (Braga) her name is carved beside that of Tongoenabiagus over a spring-fed relief.

sources.reference: Fonte do Ídolo inscription, Braga (1st c. AD); Nabia votive epigraphy

lusitanian_tongoenabiagus.name: Oath and spring cult at the Fonte do Ídolo
lusitanian_tongoenabiagus.notes: At the 1st-century Braga spring-shrine the dedicator Celicus Fronto of Arcobriga carved an offering 'Tongoe Nabiagoi' beside Nabia; the theonym is linked to *tong- ('to swear', cf. Old Irish tongu), suggesting oaths sworn at the sacred water.

sources.reference: Fonte do Ídolo inscription, Braga (TONGOE NABIAGOI / CELICVS FRONTO ARCOBRIGENSIS)

luwian_tarhunz.name: Storm-god cult at Aleppo
luwian_tarhunz.notes: Tarhunz's foremost cult centre was the temple of the storm-god at Aleppo, with worship reaching back into the Bronze Age and continuing through the Iron Age Syro-Anatolian states.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Tarḫunz'; 'Luwian religion'

luwian_arma.name: Lunar cult merged with Sin of Harran
luwian_arma.notes: In the Iron Age the cult of Arma fused with that of the moon-god Sin of Harran ('Harranian Arma'); his popularity is shown by the abundance of theophoric names such as Armaziti ('Man of Arma').

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Arma (deity)'

lycian_lada.name: Cult of Eni Mahanahi at the Letoon
lycian_lada.notes: As 'mother of this sanctuary', Lada (Leto) was the chief deity of the federal Letoon shrine near Xanthos, worshipped at a spring-fed temple beside those of her children Ertemi and the third god; cult decrees were proclaimed there (cf. the Letoon trilingual).

sources.reference: Letoon trilingual inscription (Lycian/Greek/Aramaic), Xanthos; Lycian dedications to eni mahanahi

lycian_ertemi.name: Cult at the Letoon alongside Leto
lycian_ertemi.notes: Ertemi (the Lycian Artemis), daughter of Lada, was worshipped in her own temple within the Letoon temenos near Xanthos, and shared a precinct with Maliya per the Xanthos material.

sources.reference: Letoon temple inscriptions and dedications, Xanthos

lycian_twelve_gods.name: Votive relief cult of the Twelve Gods
lycian_twelve_gods.notes: More than fifty near-identical Roman-period reliefs (2nd-4th c. AD) from across Lycia depict twelve spear-bearing gods above twelve dogs, dedicated by named worshippers; the densest concentration is at Komba (Gömbe), probably the cult's centre.

sources.reference: G. Renberg, 'Unexplored Aspects of the Lycian Twelve Gods Reliefs', Epigraphica Anatolica 47 (2014); Harvard Art Museums votive relief 287005

lydian_artimus.name: Sanctuary of Artemis at Sardis
lydian_artimus.notes: The most-attested Lydian deity had a sanctuary at Sardis from at least the 6th century BC (archaic dedications and a cult-image foundation); her name appears in Lydian-language inscriptions on the site and in funerary curse formulae.

sources.reference: Lydian inscriptions of the Artemis sanctuary, Sardis; Sardis Expedition (Greenewalt, 'Gods of Lydia')

lydian_kuvava.name: Metroac cult at Sardis
lydian_kuvava.notes: Kuvava/Kybebe was worshipped at Sardis as tutelary mother-goddess; 6th-century sculpture of the lion-attended goddess and blocks from a later metroon survive, and per Hutter her cult was gradually displaced by Phrygian Cybele.

sources.reference: Greenewalt, 'Gods of Lydia' (Sardis Expedition); Hutter, in Melchert (ed.), The Luwians (2003)

luo_nyasaye.name: Sacrifice at sacred places (hembko)
luo_nyasaye.notes: The Luo offered spotless animals to Nyasaye at sacred shrines, trees, great rocks, hills and beside Lake Victoria, especially in times of calamity (dera), to propitiate the supernatural and secure prosperity.

sources.reference: Exploring-Africa, 'Luo religious beliefs'; IJRISS, 'Elements of Luo Traditional Sacrifice'

luo_ramogi.name: Shrine-rites at Got Ramogi (Lwanda Asumbi)
luo_ramogi.notes: At the Ramogi Hills the shrine Lwanda Asumbi and a network of hembko received sacrifices during severe calamities (dera); Got Ramogi remains a venerated ancestral heritage site.

sources.reference: IJISRT, 'Luo Cultural Shrines: The Hembko of Got Ramogi, Kenya' (2024)

luo_luanda_magere.name: Veneration at the Sidho shrine-stone
luo_luanda_magere.notes: At Sidho near Awasi a revered stone marks where Luanda Magere is said to have turned to rock; warriors traditionally sharpened their blades there before battle, and people still perform rituals and prayers at the site.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Luanda Magere'; National Museums of Kenya

maasai_enkai.name: Cattle-blessing and rain petitions to Enkai
maasai_enkai.notes: The Maasai address Enkai in prayer and offering for rain, fertility and the wellbeing of the cattle that Enkai is said to have lowered to them down the roots of the sacred fig (Ficus natalensis); the tree itself is held sacred for this reason.

sources.reference: Religion Wiki, 'Maasai mythology'; TalkAfricana, 'Creation Story of the Maasai'

attributes.name: Figured votive plaques
attributes.notes: Endovelicus is known from carved votive plaques and bronze/terracotta figurines from his sanctuary rather than from any narrative image; surgical instruments among the finds underline his healing role.

sources.reference: Votive plaques and figurines, São Miguel da Mota sanctuary
Votive boar sculptures dedicated at São Miguel da Mota
Wikipedia, 'Endovelicus' (chthonic/healing associations with serpents)

attributes.name: Goat welded to a votive plaque
attributes.notes: Her characteristic image is a small goat figure fixed to an inscribed plaque, found in sanctuaries of Cáceres province; the goat is her emblem rather than a narrative attribute.

sources.reference: Votive goat-plaques, Santa Lucía del Trampal / Malpartida / Herguijuela
Ataecina votive goat-plaques

attributes.name: Crescent-moon helmet
attributes.notes: Arma is shown as a winged, bearded god wearing a helmet topped with a crescent moon; his hieroglyphic name is written with a lunette.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Arma (deity)'

attributes.name: Shoulder wings
attributes.notes: Late iconography gives the moon-god wings rising from his shoulders.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Arma (deity)'

attributes.name: Axe/hammer and thunderbolt bundle
attributes.notes: Tarhunz is depicted striding with a double-axe or hammer and a bundle of thunderbolts, often driving a horse-drawn chariot; as the vineyard-god he carries grapes and grain.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Tarḫunz'; 'Luwian religion'
Wikipedia, 'Tarḫunz' (storm-god seated on / accompanied by a bull)
Wikipedia, 'Tarḫunz' (Tarhunza of the Vineyard with grape-bunches)

attributes.name: Stag-antler hieroglyph (CERVUS)
attributes.notes: Runtiya's name is written with the deer/antler logogram, and he is shown armed with bow and arrow standing upon a stag.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Runtiya'
Wikipedia, 'Runtiya'

attributes.name: Winged sun-disc
attributes.notes: The Luwian sun-god is represented by the winged sun-disc, signalling his passage across the heavens.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Luwian religion'
Wikipedia, 'Iyarri' (archer plague-god associated with the lion)

attributes.name: Mirror and pomegranate
attributes.notes: In Neo-Hittite reliefs Kuvava/Kubaba is seated on a lion-throne wearing a polos and veil, holding a mirror (magic/divination) in one hand and a pomegranate (fertility) in the other, beneath a winged disc.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Kubaba (goddess)'; Carchemish reliefs
Wikipedia, 'Kubaba (goddess)'; lion-supported throne
Wikipedia, 'Kubaba (goddess)'

attributes.name: Enthroned between lions
attributes.notes: The Lydian mother-goddess is shown as a seated female figure flanked or accompanied by lions, in the manner of Phrygian Cybele.

sources.reference: Greenewalt, 'Gods of Lydia' (Sardis Expedition); 6th-c. BC Sardis sculpture
Greenewalt, 'Gods of Lydia'

attributes.name: Twelve spear-bearing gods over twelve dogs
attributes.notes: The standard relief divides into an upper frieze of twelve frontal armed males holding spears and a lower frieze of twelve dogs, one beneath each god, with the dedicator named between.

sources.reference: G. Renberg, Epigraphica Anatolica 47 (2014); Harvard Art Museums relief 287005
Lycian Twelve Gods reliefs

attributes.name: Bruised, one-eyed face
attributes.notes: After her quarrel with the sun Enkai, Olapa shows a wounded, scarred face with one eye struck out, visible on the full moon; the sun in turn shines too bright to look at to hide his own wound.

sources.reference: A. C. Hollis, The Masai: Their Language and Folklore (1905), sun-and-moon narrative

sacredPlants.name: Sacred fig (Ficus natalensis)
sacredPlants.notes: Enkai is said to have let the cattle down to the Maasai along the roots/vine of the sacred fig, which is therefore held sacred.

sources.reference: Religion Wiki, 'Maasai mythology'; TalkAfricana, 'Creation Story of the Maasai'
